questions.problem:
Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2{t}^{2},\,y=t+{t}^{3}
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}) \\  & =4t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+{t}^{3})(4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,1].$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t+4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot {\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\,|}_{0}^{1}+4\cdot {\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}\,|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(\frac{1}{3}-0)+4(\frac{1}{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{5} \\  & =\frac{32}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2{e}^{-t},\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{-t}) \\  & =-2{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-2{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [0,\pi ].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-(-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t)=6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=({t}^{2}-1){e}^{t},\,y={t}^{3}+1
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [1,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({t}^{2}-1){e}^{t}) \\  & =2t{e}^{t}+({t}^{2}-1){e}^{t} \\  & =({t}^{2}+2t-1){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{3}+1)({t}^{2}+2t-1){e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [1,2].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A={\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{3}+1)({t}^{2}+2t-1){e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t,\,y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$ Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$ and $t\ge 0.$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & ⇒ & v=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t| \\  & =|\,-\frac{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\,| \\  & =|\,-\frac{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}\,| \\  & =|\,-\frac{\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2}+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)\,| \\  & =|\,\frac{\pi }{4}\,| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
